title: Demonstrate an understanding of establishing a vineyard

lessons.title: Planning and planting a new vineyard
lessons.html:
Planning and planting a new vineyard

Establishing a vineyard means getting a new vineyard planted and growing well in its first years. It takes careful planning, because the vines will stay for many years.

The plan

The farm manager decides:

  • the site and the soil preparation needed;
  • the cultivar and rootstock for each block;
  • the row direction, row width and space between vines;
  • the trellis system and the irrigation system;
  • when to plant, usually in late winter or early spring before the buds grow.

Plant material

Vines are bought from a registered nursery as grafted, rooted plants. Certified plant material is tested to be free of the main virus diseases. When the vines arrive:

  • check that the cultivar and rootstock on the labels are correct;
  • keep the roots moist and cool, out of sun and wind;
  • store them as the nursery says until planting.

Planting steps

  1. Mark each planting spot along the row with the stake.
  2. Trim the roots and shoot as your supervisor shows you, if the farm does this.
  3. Dig a hole big enough for the roots to spread without bending upwards.
  4. Hold the vine upright next to the stake. The graft union (the joint) must be above the soil, so the scion does not make its own roots.
  5. Fill soil around the roots and press it firmly with your foot.
  6. Water each vine well straight after planting, even if the soil is moist.
  7. Some farms cover the young vine with a plastic sleeve or a small soil heap to protect it. Follow the farm's method.

Plant one block at a time and do not mix up labels. Write down the block, cultivar, rootstock, number of vines and date.

lessons.title: Caring for young vines
lessons.html:
Caring for young vines

The first two to three years decide how strong and productive the vineyard will be. Young vines have small roots and need extra care.

Water

Young vines dry out quickly. Check soil moisture often and irrigate as the manager plans. Check that every vine gets water: look for blocked drippers and leaking pipes.

Weeds

Weeds compete strongly with small vines for water and nutrients. Keep the area around each vine clean by hand or hoe. Be careful not to damage the young stem or roots. If herbicides are used, only trained workers apply them, and the young vines must be protected from spray, for example with plastic sleeves.

Training the young vine

  • Choose the strongest shoot and tie it loosely to the stake so it grows straight up.
  • Remove the other shoots as instructed.
  • Remove suckers that grow from the rootstock below the graft.
  • Tie gently. Ties that are too tight cut into the stem as it grows.

The aim is a straight, strong trunk that reaches the cordon wire.

Pests and diseases

Watch for cutworms and snails that eat young shoots, for leaf diseases, and for damage from hares, porcupines or buck. Report problems to your supervisor quickly.

Replacing dead vines

Count the vines in each row. Mark dead or weak vines so they can be replaced in the next planting season. Gaps mean less crop for many years.

No crop at first

Young vines should not carry a full crop. The farm usually removes bunches in the first year or two so the vine puts its energy into roots and trunk.

Key points

  • Plan the site, cultivar, rootstock, spacing, trellis and irrigation before planting.
  • Use certified vines from a registered nursery and keep the roots moist.
  • Plant with the graft union above the soil and water well straight after.
  • Keep young vines watered and free of weeds; remove suckers.
  • Train one strong shoot up the stake to form the trunk.
